docs.title: OER Evaluator
docs.text:
Title: OER Evaluator: Evaluating and Improving Open Educational Resources with AI Agents

Target Audience: Teachers (K-12 and college), instructional designers, librarians, and OER coordinators who select, adapt, or create open educational resources (OER)

Prerequisites: None. Readers should be comfortable using a web browser and a word processor. Experience with an AI chat assistant is helpful but not required; the book teaches the AI-agent skills it uses.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Open educational resources (OER) are teaching and learning materials that carry an open license, so anyone can retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute them. Finding OER is easy. Knowing whether a resource is good, and whether it can actually be reused in another course, is hard. A careful manual review of one textbook can take hours, and reviewers working from different checklists reach different conclusions.

This course teaches a repeatable method for judging an OER on 10 metrics worth 10 points each: five for quality and five for reusability. The quality metrics are accuracy and currency, alignment to learning outcomes, readability, accessibility, and practice with feedback. The reusability metrics are open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, and portability. Readers learn to score a resource by hand, then to direct an AI agent to make the first pass, check the agent's evidence, and decide which findings to accept, correct, or reject. Readers also learn the limits of agent scoring: invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores.

The course then turns evaluation into improvement. Readers use AI agents to raise a resource's score by adding alt text, splitting a long chapter into reusable modules, writing metadata, generating practice questions, and building interactive simulations (MicroSims). Finally, readers learn to test whether a change helped. The main method is a manual A/B test with students, in which one group uses the original resource and another uses the improved version and the results are compared. Those results are then used to check and calibrate the automated scores, which is how AI skills for automated assessment of OER textbooks are validated.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
• What OER are, the 5R permissions, and how OER differ from free or public-domain content
  • Open licenses: the Creative Commons family, license compatibility, and attribution
  • Why OER quality varies and what quality means for a learner
  • The 10-metric rubric: scoring scales, evidence, and the 100-point total
  • Quality metrics: accuracy and currency, alignment to learning outcomes, readability, accessibility, and practice with feedback
  • Reusability metrics: open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, and portability
  • Manual evaluation: scoring a resource by hand and recording evidence
  • AI-agent evaluation: writing prompts and skills that score a resource and cite evidence
  • Checking agent output: hallucinated citations, license misreads, and overconfident scores
  • Calibrating agents against human reviewers and measuring agreement
  • Improving a resource with AI agents, one metric at a time
  • Designing reusable components: modular chapters, quizzes, glossaries, and MicroSims
  • Metadata standards (such as Dublin Core) and open formats for editable source
  • Accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1 AA) for text, images, video, and interactive content
  • Manual A/B testing of an OER with students: design, sampling, and ethics
  • Analyzing A/B test results and comparing them with rubric scores
  • Publishing, sharing, and maintaining improved OER, including repositories and version control
  • Training others and earning a certificate in OER quality evaluation with AI agents

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Writing a complete textbook from scratch or full instructional design for a course
  • Copyright law beyond what is needed to read and apply open licenses
  • Training or fine-tuning AI models; the course uses existing AI agents
  • Programming beyond simple prompts, Markdown, and HTML needed to publish a resource
  • Learning management system (LMS) administration and procurement of commercial materials
  • Statistical methods beyond basic comparisons of two groups

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define open educational resource and list the 5R permissions: retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute
  • Name the 10 metrics of the rubric and identify which five measure quality and which five measure reusability
  • Recall the Creative Commons license elements (BY, SA, NC, ND) and the meaning of each
  • List the required fields of a metadata record, such as title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description
  • Identify common AI-agent errors, including invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores
  • State the purpose of an A/B test and name its two groups

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain why a resource can be high quality but low in reusability, and the reverse, using examples
  • Describe how each of the 10 metrics is scored and what evidence supports a score
  • Explain how an AI agent scores a resource against a rubric and why a human must check its evidence
  • Summarize how open licenses combine and why some combinations are incompatible
  • Explain how modular content and editable source files make a resource easier to reuse
  • Describe how accessibility features, such as alt text and heading structure, help learners

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Score a sample OER on all 10 metrics by hand and record evidence for each score
  • Write an AI-agent prompt that scores a resource against the rubric and returns evidence
  • Add alt text, headings, and captions to a resource so it meets WCAG 2.1 AA
  • Record complete metadata and a license statement for an existing resource
  • Split a long chapter into modules that each stand alone and can be embedded elsewhere
  • Run a small A/B test with two groups of students and record the outcomes

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Compare a teacher's scores with an agent's scores and find where they differ by more than 3 points
  • Trace a low total score back to the specific metrics and passages that caused it
  • Classify the errors in an agent's evaluation as factual, license, citation, or scoring errors
  • Examine a resource's licenses and attributions to find conflicts that block reuse
  • Compare A/B test results with rubric scores to find which metrics predict learner outcomes
  • Differentiate improvements that raise the score from improvements that raise learning

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Judge whether an OER is ready to adopt, needs revision, or should be rejected, and justify the decision
  • Critique an agent's evaluation and decide which findings to accept, correct, or reject
  • Assess whether a revised resource gained on at least two quality and two reusability metrics
  • Evaluate the reliability of the rubric by checking agreement between reviewers and agents
  • Appraise the design of an A/B test for fairness, sample size, and student privacy
  • Defend an adoption recommendation to a department or district using rubric evidence

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design a reusable component, such as a quiz, glossary, or MicroSim, that other teachers can embed under an open license
  • Build an AI-agent skill that evaluates OER automatically and reports scores with evidence
  • Produce an improved version of an existing OER and publish it with metadata
  • Design and run an A/B test that compares an original resource with its improved version
  • Develop a training workshop that teaches colleagues to evaluate OER with AI agents
  • Capstone project: evaluate one OER from your own subject, use AI agents to improve it on at least two quality and two reusability metrics, test the change with students, and publish the result under a CC BY license

Chapters are added by the book-chapter-generator skill once the learning graph is complete; their content is filled in by the chapter-content-generator skill.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in OER Evaluator depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text: Skill: Course Description Analyzer, version 0.05 Assessed file: Course Description

docs.title: Overall Score: 98/100
docs.text: Quality rating: Excellent. Ready for learning graph generation.

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points earned Points possible Notes Title 5 5 Clear and descriptive Target Audience 4 5 Specific roles named, but the range from K-12 teachers to librarians is broad Prerequisites 5 5 Stated as "None", with a note on helpful experience Main Topics Covered 9 10 Comprehensive, but 18 topics is above the ideal 5 to 10 Topics Excluded 5 5 Six clear boundaries Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After completing this course, students will be able to:" Remember Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Understand Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Apply Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Analyze Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Evaluate Level 10 10 Six specific outcomes Create Level 10 10 Six outcomes plus a capstone project Descriptive Context 5 5 Three paragraphs on why and how Total 98 100

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
• Target Audience (4 of 5): four roles are named (K-12 teachers, college instructors, instructional designers, librarians and OER coordinators). The reading level and examples may need to favor one group. This slightly weakens the audience signal the learning graph uses to set concept depth.
  • Main Topics (9 of 10): the 18 topics are all relevant, but several overlap, such as the two metric topics and the two A/B testing topics. Overlap can produce duplicate concepts in the graph.

Two gaps are not scored by the rubric but matter for the book:

  • The 10 metrics have no scoring scale yet. The description names them and gives 10 points each, but does not say what earns a 10, a 5, or a 0. Chapters and the AI-agent prompts will need this.
  • The metrics are a proposal. They were drafted for the MNOP Pathfinder grant proposal, not taken from a published standard. The author should confirm or revise them.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Define the scoring scale for each metric, with a short description of a 10, a 5, and a 0. This is the highest-value addition, because most chapters and sims depend on it.
  2. Merge overlapping topics if the learning graph comes out with duplicate concepts. For example, combine "Manual A/B testing" and "Analyzing A/B test results".
  3. Pick a primary audience for examples, for instance K-12 teachers, and note that the other roles can follow the same method.
  4. Cite external standards where the rubric borrows from them: the 5R permissions, WCAG 2.1 AA, Dublin Core, and Creative Commons licenses.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated concepts: about 220 to 280.

  • The 18 topics, at roughly 10 to 15 learnable concepts each, give about 180 to 270.
  • The 10 metrics each suggest several concepts of their own, such as the evidence a score needs, common failure cases, and fixes.
  • The Bloom's outcomes add process concepts, such as calibration, agreement, and error types.
  • This is an estimate. The learning-graph generator may find fewer after removing duplicates.

The description should support the 200-concept goal. If the generator falls short, the first place to add detail is the metric scoring scales.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: The score is at least 85, so the course description is ready to proceed with learning graph generation. Run the learning-graph-generator skill next.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Sample OER Evaluator Workshop Resources
docs.text:
These sample materials support a one-day workshop that trains teachers to evaluate open educational resources (OER) for quality and reusability with AI agents, and then to use those agents to improve an OER they already teach with. Teachers who finish the follow-up work earn the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents.

  • Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule: the 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. agenda for about 20 teachers, with what each session produces and what to do before and after the day.
  • Sample Rubric Worksheet: a fill-in worksheet that scores one OER on five quality and five reusability metrics, compares teacher and AI-agent scores, logs agent findings, and lists the certificate requirements.
  • Grant-Period Timeline: a sample November 2026 to May 2027 timeline, from building the rubric and recruiting teachers through the training day, certificate work, classroom A/B tests, and the final report.

docs.title: Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule
docs.text:
This workshop trains teachers to evaluate open educational resources (OER) for quality and reusability with AI agents, and then to use those agents to improve an OER they already teach with. Teachers arrive with one OER from their own subject and leave with an improved, openly licensed component and a checklist for earning the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents.

The day runs 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and is designed for about 20 teachers. Every session uses the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Before the Workshop
docs.text:
Each teacher should:

  • Choose one OER they already use, such as a textbook chapter, a unit, a quiz, or an interactive simulation.
  • Bring a laptop with access to an AI agent tool.
  • Print or download the Sample Rubric Worksheet.

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text: Time Session What teachers leave with 8:30 to 9:00 Check-in and setup: log in to the AI tools and load the OER each teacher brought A working agent session 9:00 to 9:45 Why quality and reusability matter: the 10 metrics and how each is scored Rubric card 9:45 to 10:45 Calibration: pairs score a sample OER by hand, then run the agent and compare Hand and agent scores, with gaps explained 10:45 to 11:00 Break 11:00 to 12:00 Checking the agent: spot invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores A verified evaluation of the sample 12:00 to 12:45 Lunch 12:45 to 2:15 Improvement challenge: use agents to raise one component's score by adding alt text, splitting content into reusable modules, writing metadata, generating practice questions, or building a simulation An improved component and its new score 2:15 to 2:30 Break 2:30 to 3:15 Peer review and publishing: swap and re-score each other's work, then publish under a CC BY license A published, openly licensed component 3:15 to 3:30 Next steps: certificate requirements and exit survey Certificate checklist

docs.title: After the Workshop
docs.text:
Teachers have 30 days to finish the certificate work described at the end of the Sample Rubric Worksheet. A reviewer checks each submission against the rubric before the certificate is issued.

The workshop sits inside a longer program, from building the rubric through the final report. See the Grant-Period Timeline.

docs.title: Sample Rubric Worksheet
docs.text:
This worksheet scores one open educational resource (OER) out of 100 points: 50 for quality and 50 for reusability, with 10 points per metric. Score each metric yourself, then record the AI agent's score beside yours so you can see where you and the agent disagree.

The reusability metrics follow the 5R permissions of open content: the right to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. These are sample metrics; they will be aligned with the chapters of this book as they are written.

Use it with the Sample One-Day Workshop Schedule.

docs.title: Resource Being Reviewed
docs.text: Field Entry Title URL License Subject and grade level Component reviewed (chapter, unit, quiz, or simulation) Reviewer Date

docs.title: Part 1: Quality (50 points)
docs.text: Metric What to check Your score (0 to 10) Agent score (0 to 10) Evidence Accuracy and currency Facts match cited sources; sources and data are current Alignment Each section maps to a stated learning outcome; Bloom's levels range from remember to create Readability Reading level fits the audience; terms are defined before use Accessibility Alt text, heading structure, captions, and color contrast (WCAG 2.1 AA) Practice with feedback Quizzes, worked examples, or interactive simulations that give feedback

docs.title: Part 2: Reusability (50 points)
docs.text: Metric What to check Your score (0 to 10) Agent score (0 to 10) Evidence Open license License stated on every component; attributions complete; CC BY preferred Modularity Each section, quiz, or simulation stands alone and can be embedded elsewhere Metadata Title, author, subject, grade level, license, and description recorded (Dublin Core) Editable source Source in an editable format such as Markdown, HTML, or a word-processing file, not only PDF Portability Runs in a browser with no login; embeddable by link or iframe

docs.title: Totals
docs.text: Part Your score Agent score Score after improvement Quality (out of 50) Reusability (out of 50) Total (out of 100)

docs.title: Calibration: Where You and the Agent Disagree
docs.text:
List every metric where your score and the agent's score differ by more than 3 points, and explain which score you trust and why.

Metric Your score Agent score Explanation

docs.title: Agent Findings Log
docs.text:
AI agents make confident mistakes, such as invented citations, misread licenses, and overconfident scores. Record each agent finding and what you did with it.

Agent finding Accepted, corrected, or rejected Why

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
To earn the Certificate of OER Quality Evaluation Using AI Agents, a teacher:

  1. Attends the full training day.
  2. Completes the calibration exercise and explains every metric where their score and the agent's differ by more than 3 points.
  3. Submits an evaluation of one OER from their own subject, scored on all 10 metrics, with evidence for each score and a note on every agent finding they accepted, corrected, or rejected.
  4. Publishes one improved component under a CC BY license, with metadata, that gains on at least two quality and two reusability metrics.
  5. Submits both within 30 days of the workshop. A reviewer checks each submission against this rubric.
